name: saints

attributes.attribute: a figure whose memory the Catholic Church shaped through a three-stage process
an Irish saint believed by some to come from a Celtic goddess of the same name

sources: Kelly, Sean, and Rosemary Rogers. Saints Preserve Us! (New York: Random House, 1993).
Monaghan, Patricia. The Encyclopedia of Celtic Mythology and Folklore. Checkmark Books, 2008.
text: Saints are folkloric figures. The Catholic Church fixed the way a person becomes a saint. A candidate moves through three stages. The Church calls a candidate venerable, then blessed, then saint. The Church set this process in the 10th century under Pope John XV. Before that, popular acclaim made a saint. That open path let some pagan divinities into the calendar. Each gained the title saint before his or her name. The god Priapus was once listed this way. Reform removed him in 1983. Other doubtful saints remain. Saint Brigit keeps a place in the church calendar. Brigit resembles a Celtic goddess of the same name. Real people also became saints. Legend added marvels to their lives. Saint Ailbe was said to be suckled by wolves. Saint Flannan sailed to Rome in a boat made of stone. Saint Cury lived off a self-renewing fish. King Arthur's Welsh friend Saint Gwynllyw joined their company. Those marvels may come from retelling that merged the stories of saints, divinities, and fairies.
